596.title: By the mount and the book
596.word: By the mount and the book
596.hook: by the mount, and a book inscribed on open parchment (52:1–3)
596.howItsDone: Muslims handle the Qur'an with care: many perform ablution before touching the Arabic text, keep it on a high shelf, and say bismillah before reading; the Prophet's recitation of At-Tur in the sunset prayer is often followed by imams.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was 'ibadah, worship in the widest sense, and your line was made for worship. Which ordinary task did you turn, with an intention? Day five hundred ninety-six.

A young man from Mecca named Jubayr ibn Mut'im came to Medina after the battle of Badr, on business about prisoners. He wasn't a Muslim. At sunset he heard the Prophet ﷺ leading the prayer, reciting aloud. Years later, Jubayr described that moment, and his words are in Sahih al-Bukhari: when the recitation reached certain verses, he said, my heart nearly flew. The surah he heard was At-Tur, the Mount. Today we open it.

At-Tur begins, like yesterday's surah, with oaths. Pickthall's translation: "By the Mount, And a Scripture inscribed On fine parchment unrolled." The Mount, at-Tur, is understood by the commentators as Mount Sinai, the mountain where Musa heard Allah speak. The Arabic word tur means a mountain, and in the Qur'an it points again and again to that one. Then a book: kitabin mastur, written in lines, on raqqin manshur, parchment spread open. Raqq is fine, thin skin prepared for writing, the surface kept for texts meant to last. Commentators differ on which book. Some say the Torah given at that mountain. Some say the Qur'an. Some say the preserved tablet in heaven, or the records of deeds that every person will see unrolled. The verse doesn't specify, and the honest answer is that the scholars hold several views. What's clear is the pairing: a mountain and a page. A place where revelation happened, and the writing that carries it to people who weren't there. Then the oaths continue: by the frequented House, by the roof raised high, by the swelling sea. And they're answered: the punishment of your Lord will surely come. Jubayr's heart nearly flew a little later in the surah, at verses that ask: were they created out of nothing, or are they the creators? It was a question, not an argument. Reports say it was the first time faith settled in his heart, and he later became a Muslim. A recited page did that, in the half-light, to a man who came only for business.
screen: `AT-TUR: THE MOUNT OF MUSA.` · `RAQQ: PARCHMENT SPREAD OPEN.` · `WHICH BOOK? SEVERAL VIEWS.` · `A MOUNTAIN AND A PAGE.`

segments.voice: The practice: open a book with respect. If there's a book you value near you, a Qur'an, a Bible, a book of poems, a family journal, bring it close. If not, picture one. Before you open it, pause. Notice its weight, the cover, the edges of the pages. Then open it slowly, as if it were parchment that might tear. Read one line. Just one. If you pray, you can say bismillah before you open it. The bell holds the time.
By the mount and the book. The oaths that open At-Tur: Mount Sinai, where Musa heard, and a book written in lines on parchment spread open. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: by the mount. Today, open one book you love on purpose, slowly, and read a single line as if it were rare. Day five hundred ninety-six.

597.title: When the stars retreat
597.hook: glorify Him when you rise and at the retreat of the stars (52:48–49)
597.howItsDone: Many Muslims pray two short voluntary units before the obligatory dawn prayer, and say subhanallah, often thirty-three times, after prayers and in the early morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, by the mount and the book, and your line was by the mount. Which book did you open slowly, and what was the line? Day five hundred ninety-seven.

If you've ever been awake at the very end of the night, you know the moment. The sky is still dark, but something has shifted. The faint stars go first. Then the brighter ones, one by one, as if someone were walking through a house turning off lamps. Birds start before there's any light to speak of. It lasts only a few minutes. Surah At-Tur ends exactly there, at that moment, and it tells the Prophet ﷺ what to do with it.
screen: `THE STARS GO OUT, ONE BY ONE.`

segments.voice: The last two verses of At-Tur begin with comfort. Wait patiently for your Lord's decree, it says to the Prophet, for you are in Our sight. The Arabic is bi-a'yunina, literally within Our eyes: watched over, never out of view. Then the instruction, in Pickthall's translation: "And in the night-time also hymn His praise, and at the setting of the stars." Idbar an-nujum: the turning back of the stars, their retreat as dawn comes. Two moments of glorifying, tasbih, are named across these verses: when you rise, and when the stars withdraw. Commentators connected idbar an-nujum with the two short units of prayer before the dawn prayer, the sunnah of Fajr. A report attributed to Ibn 'Abbas says so, and many followed him. And the hadith tradition treats those two units with unusual tenderness. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says the two units before dawn are better than the world and everything in it. 'A'ishah reported, in Bukhari, that he was never more regular in any voluntary prayer than in those two. Notice the shape of the verse. It doesn't say glorify Him in the bright, busy middle of the day. It says, in effect: at the edges. When you've just risen and when the night is letting go. The hours when nobody needs you yet. The word tasbih comes from the root s-b-h, which also carries the sense of swimming, moving swiftly through. Subhanallah: glory be to Allah, far above every flaw. Said as the stars fade, it's a way of meeting the day before the day starts asking things of you.
screen: `BI-A'YUNINA: WITHIN OUR EYES.` · `IDBAR AN-NUJUM: THE STARS TURN BACK.` · `THE TWO UNITS BEFORE DAWN.` · `PRAISE AT THE EDGES OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: The practice is a tasbih before dawn. You can rehearse it now, and keep it tomorrow. Sit, and breathe. Picture waking before the light, the sky just beginning to thin. With each slow breath, say subhanallah quietly, glory to Allah. Count on your fingers if you like. If you don't pray, simply hold the picture of the stars going out, one by one, and let your breath slow with them. Set an alarm for a few minutes before sunrise tomorrow. The bell holds the time.
When the stars retreat. Idbar an-nujum: the last moment of night in 52:49, linked by commentators to the two units of prayer before dawn. Today's word.
Your line: as the stars fade. Tomorrow, try to be awake as the last stars go, and give the first minute to praise or to stillness. Day five hundred ninety-seven.

598.title: Not from desire
598.hook: by the star, your companion is not astray, nor does he speak from desire (53:1–3)
598.tomorrow: The lote tree of the boundary
598.howItsDone: Muslims cite 53:3–4 as a basis for following the Prophet's Sunnah alongside the Qur'an, and scholars of hadith built careful methods for recording and checking his words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, when the stars retreat, and your line was as the stars fade. Were you awake for the last stars, or close to it? Day five hundred ninety-eight.

A young man named 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr used to write down everything the Prophet ﷺ said. Every word. Some men of Quraysh told him to stop: he's a human being, they said, he speaks in anger and in good moods; why write it all? So 'Abdullah stopped, and went to ask. The Prophet pointed to his own mouth and told him to keep writing. Nothing comes out of this, he said, except truth. Today's surah has a verse behind that answer.

Surah An-Najm, the Star, the fifty-third, opens with one oath. Pickthall's translation: "By the Star when it setteth, Your comrade erreth not, nor is deceived; Nor doth he speak of (his own) desire." Which star? Commentators differ. Some say the Pleiades, a star cluster the Arabs watched closely; some say a falling star; some say any star at its setting. The oath is by something going down, out of sight, while what the surah defends stays. Then: your comrade, sahibukum. Not the Prophet or the Messenger, but your companion, the man you've known for forty years, who grew up among you. You know he isn't a liar. Then the key line: wa ma yantiqu 'anil-hawa. Nor does he speak from desire. You've met that word: hawa, the desire that pulls you along, from the day we read desire as a god. Here the surah says the one bringing the message isn't driven by it. The next verse says: it is nothing but revelation revealed. How far does that reach? Scholars have discussed it carefully. All agree it covers the Qur'an. Most hold that his teaching in religious matters, the Sunnah, also comes from revelation in a broader sense, which is why hadith became a source of law. And many note the reports where he gave an opinion in worldly matters, like how to pollinate date palms, and said: you know better the affairs of your world. So the verse isn't a claim that he never had a personal view. It's a claim about the message: it isn't self-serving, and it isn't his wanting dressed up as revelation.
screen: `BY THE STAR AS IT SETS.` · `SAHIBUKUM: THE COMPANION YOU KNOW.` · `NOT FROM HAWA, BUT REVELATION.` · `HOW FAR IT REACHES: SCHOLARS WEIGH IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: speak without self-interest once. Sit, and breathe. Think of a conversation coming up today: advice you'll give, a recommendation, a review, an opinion at work. Ask yourself honestly where your words might lean toward what you want: looking good, winning, getting your way. Choose one place to say what's true and useful for the other person, even if it gains you nothing. If you pray, you can ask for an honest tongue. The bell holds the time.
Not from desire. Ma yantiqu 'anil-hawa: in 53:3, the Prophet does not speak from his own wanting; the message is revelation. Today's word.
Your line: not from desire. Today, before you give one piece of advice, check whether it serves them or you, and adjust it. Day five hundred ninety-eight.

599.title: The lote tree of the boundary
599.word: The lote tree of the boundary
599.hook: he saw Jibril at the lote tree of the utmost boundary, near the garden (53:13–15)
599.howItsDone: Muslims remember the Isra' and Mi'raj, often on the 27th of Rajab, retelling the journey to the lote tree and the gift of the five daily prayers; sidr leaves are still used in many places for washing the dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, not from desire, and your line was the same: not from desire. Where did you give advice that served them more than you? Day five hundred ninety-nine.

In the dry country of Arabia there's a hardy tree called the sidr, the lote tree. Thorny branches, small leaves, a little fruit like a tart crabapple. It grows where almost nothing else does, and its shade has saved travelers' lives. Its leaves are still used in many places to wash the bodies of the dead. An ordinary desert tree. And the Qur'an puts one at the very edge of creation, at the farthest point anything created can reach.

Surah An-Najm describes two times the Prophet ﷺ saw the angel Jibril in his true form. The first was on the horizon, near the beginning. The second, in Pickthall's translation: "And verily he saw him yet another time By the lote-tree of the utmost boundary, Nigh unto which is the Garden of Abode." Sidrat al-muntaha. Muntaha means the end point, the furthest limit. Commentators explain it as the place beyond which no created being passes, where the knowledge of creatures stops. Most link this second sighting to the Night Journey and Ascension, the Isra' and Mi'raj, when the Prophet was taken through the heavens. 'A'ishah and Ibn Mas'ud both said, in reports in the two Sahihs, that what he saw at the tree was Jibril, as he truly is; Ibn Mas'ud reported six hundred wings. The hadith of the Ascension in Bukhari describes the tree itself: fruits like great clay jars, leaves like elephants' ears, and rivers flowing from its roots. Then the surah says something covered the tree, a covering it doesn't name, and the commentators say plainly that it's beyond description. And then a line many readers find the most moving in the passage: the sight did not swerve, nor did it go beyond. At the edge of everything, he didn't look away, and he didn't grab for more than he was shown. Notice the choice of image. Not a palace or a throne at the boundary, but a tree, the kind that gives shade in hard places. The farthest point of creation is marked by something familiar.
screen: `JIBRIL, SEEN A SECOND TIME.` · `SIDRAT AL-MUNTAHA: THE FARTHEST LIMIT.` · `FRUIT LIKE JARS, LEAVES LIKE EARS.` · `THE SIGHT DID NOT SWERVE.`

segments.voice: The practice: sit at a boundary. If you can, go to an edge: a doorstep, a window, the shore, the end of a street where the fields begin. If you can't, picture one. Sit with one foot on each side, inside and out, here and beyond. Notice the line. Then do what the verse describes: look steadily, without swerving, and without reaching for more than what's in front of you. If you pray, you can ask for that steadiness. The bell holds the time.
The lote tree of the boundary. Sidrat al-muntaha: the tree at the farthest limit of creation, where the Prophet saw Jibril a second time. Today's word.
screen: `THE LOTE TREE OF THE BOUNDARY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the farthest tree. Today, when you pass a tree, let it remind you that the edge of everything is marked by something that gives shade. Day five hundred ninety-nine.

600.title: Only what he strives for
600.hook: a person has only what he strives for, and his striving will be seen (53:39–40)
600.howItsDone: Pilgrims perform the sa'y, walking seven times between Safa and Marwah in memory of Hajar; Muslims also give charity and pray on behalf of parents who have died, as hadith describe.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lote tree of the boundary, and your line was the farthest tree. Did a tree, or an edge, stop you for a moment? Day six hundred.

Day six hundred. That's a lot of mornings. Nobody gave them to you; you kept turning up. Some days with full attention, some days half-asleep, some days just pressing play so the streak wouldn't break. All of it counted. Today's verse is about exactly that: what a person ends up holding at the end. Not what they hoped for, not what they inherited, not what someone said about them. What they actually strove for.

Surah An-Najm, verses thirty-nine and forty. Pickthall's translation: "And that man hath only that for which he maketh effort, And that his effort will be seen." The word is sa'y, striving, effort, going toward something on purpose. If you've followed the pilgrimage, you've met it. The sa'y is the walk, seven times, between the hills of Safa and Marwah, remembering Hajar running between them searching for water for her baby, Isma'il. Same word. Effort as a body moving toward what it needs. The verse sits in a passage the surah says was in the scrolls of Musa and of Ibrahim: that no soul carries another's burden, and that a person has only what they strive for. Two promises come out of it. First, nobody can take your effort from you, or be credited with it in your place. Second, it will be seen. Not necessarily by people. Seen. Here the scholars raise an honest question. What about charity given for the dead, or prayers for a parent who's gone? Hadith in Bukhari and Muslim say such things do reach the dead. Scholars reconcile it in different ways. Some say a righteous child is part of the parent's own striving: a hadith in Muslim names a good child who prays for you among the three things that continue after death. Others say the verse sets the rule of justice, and Allah's generosity can add to it. Either way, the core holds: what you work for is yours, and it doesn't go unwatched.
screen: `SA'Y: EFFORT TOWARD A NEED.` · `HAJAR, BETWEEN SAFA AND MARWAH.` · `YOURS, AND IT WILL BE SEEN.` · `WHAT REACHES THE DEAD? SCHOLARS WEIGH IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: strive at one thing today. Sit, and breathe. Picture Hajar's walk: back and forth between two hills, looking, not giving up. Now choose one thing today that deserves your real effort: a hard conversation, a task you keep postponing, a skill you're learning, a person who needs you. Picture yourself doing it fully, not halfway. Feel what it would be like to finish. If you pray, you can ask for strength in it. The bell holds the time.
Only what he strives for. Sa'y: in 53:39, a person has only their effort, and in 53:40, that effort will be seen. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: only what you strive for. Today, give your real effort to the one thing you chose, and let it be seen by whoever sees. Day six hundred.

601.title: The moon split
601.hook: the Hour draws near and the moon is split (54:1)
601.howItsDone: Muslims recite Surah Al-Qamar and count the splitting of the moon among the Prophet's miracles; the Prophet recited it, with Surah Qaf, in the Eid prayers, and many imams still do.

segments.voice: Yesterday, only what he strives for, and your line was only what you strive for. What did you give your real effort to? Day six hundred one.

A clear night at Mina, just outside Mecca. The moon over the mountains. A group of men from Quraysh have come to the Prophet ﷺ with a challenge: show us a sign. What happened next is reported by several Companions, in the most trusted hadith collections, and it gave the fifty-fourth surah its name: Al-Qamar, the Moon. Its first verse is only a few words long, and it holds two things together that don't obviously belong together: the end of time, and a moon.
screen: `THE END OF TIME, AND A MOON.`

segments.voice: Pickthall's translation of the first verse: "The hour drew nigh and the moon was rent in twain." Iqtarabat as-sa'ah: the Hour has come near. Wanshaqqa al-qamar: and the moon split. In Sahih al-Bukhari, 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud says he was there. The moon split into two pieces, one part over the mountain and one beyond it, and the Prophet said: bear witness. Anas ibn Malik reports that the Meccans had asked for a sign, and they were shown this. Most classical scholars read the verse this way, as an event in the Prophet's lifetime, a sign given to people who asked. A minority read the past tense as a vivid way of describing something certain to come with the Hour. Then verse two describes the reaction: if they see a sign, they turn away and say, a magic that keeps going. The surah's point isn't astronomy. It's the gap between seeing and accepting. People asked for a sign, saw one, and found a word to explain it away. Why put the moon next to the Hour? Commentators note that the Hour's nearness is a constant theme of these late surahs. The Prophet once held up two fingers side by side and said: I and the Hour were sent like these two. The moon split is presented as an early crack in the ordinary, a sign that the world's order isn't permanent. One honest note. You may see claims online that space agencies photographed proof of the split. No such confirmation exists, and the tradition never rested on one. It rests on the reports of people who said they saw it.
screen: `IBN MAS'UD: BEAR WITNESS.` · `MOST SAY: AN EVENT IN HIS LIFETIME.` · `THEY SAW A SIGN AND CALLED IT MAGIC.` · `A CRACK IN THE ORDINARY.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at the moon. Tonight, if the sky allows, step outside and find it, whatever its phase. If it's hidden, picture the last moon you remember. Look at it long enough for it to stop being familiar: a stone hanging in nothing, lit by a sun you can't see. Notice the urge to glance and move on. Stay instead. If you pray, you can say subhanallah. Now, sit with that picture. The bell holds the time.
The moon split. Inshaqqa al-qamar: the sign of 54:1, reported by Ibn Mas'ud and others, set beside the nearness of the Hour. Today's word.
Your line: the hour draws near. Tonight, when you see the moon, let it remind you that time is moving, and do one thing you've been putting off. Day six hundred one.

602.title: Easy to remember
602.hook: We have made the Qur'an easy to remember; is there any who will remember (54:17)
602.carry: is there any who will remember?
602.howItsDone: Many Muslims memorize short surahs as children for the daily prayers, and some memorize the whole Qur'an with a teacher who listens line by line; a person who has done so is called a hafiz.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Surah Al-Qamar opened with the moon split, and your line was the hour draws near. Did you find the moon, wherever it was hanging? Day six hundred two, the end of the week.

Someone reads you a phone number once. A minute later it's gone. Now think of the chorus of a song you haven't heard in ten years. It's still there, every word, and it comes back the moment the first note plays. Some words stick. Surah fifty-four, the Moon, tells one hard story after another: Nuh and the flood, the people of 'Ad and the wind, Thamud and the she-camel, the people of Lut. And between the stories, like a chorus, one line keeps coming back. It's a line about remembering, and it ends with a question.

Verse seventeen. Pickthall: "And in truth We have made the Qur'an easy to remember; but is there any that remembereth?" Then the line returns, almost word for word, in verses twenty-two, thirty-two and forty. Four times in one surah, each time after a story closes. The Arabic for we have made it easy is yassarna, from the root y-s-r, ease. And the word for remembering is dhikr, the same remembrance this path has met so often. Classical commentators read the verse two ways at once. Easy to remember: the Qur'an is easy to hold in memory. And easy for remembrance: easy to take a reminder from. History backs the first reading in an unusual way. Across the Muslim world, children and adults memorize the entire book, more than six thousand verses, and someone who has done it is called a hafiz, a keeper or guardian of it. Many memorize it before Arabic is their everyday language. The rhyme and rhythm help, and so does a teacher listening line by line. But the verse doesn't stop at the ease. It ends on a question: fa hal min muddakir, so is there anyone who will remember? The ease is offered; someone has to pick it up. And a hadith in Bukhari adds a kindness for those who find it hard. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said that the one skilled in the Qur'an will be with the noble scribes, and the one who struggles to learn it, reciting with difficulty, has a double reward. So the question isn't only for the gifted. It's put to anyone with one verse they could learn.

segments.voice: The practice: memorize one short verse. Sit, and let your breath settle. If you're Muslim, take a verse you half-know, maybe the opening of Surah Al-Ikhlas, and say it slowly, again and again, until it holds without looking. If that isn't yours, take today's line: is there any that remembereth? Say it on the out-breath a few times, then stop, and see whether it stays with you in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Easy to remember. Surah Al-Qamar says four times that the Qur'an is made easy to remember, and each time asks who will. Today's word.

Your line: is there any who will remember? This week climbed from the Mount and the fading stars, through the Star and its lote tree, to the split moon and today's chorus. Tonight, say your one verse once more before you sleep. Day six hundred two.

original.note: Arabic: so is there anyone who will remember? The question that closes the chorus of Surah Al-Qamar.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line saying the Qur'an is easy.
what it means: a chorus, four times in one surah, offering ease and then asking who will take it up.
what a scholar hears: yassarna li-dh-dhikr can mean easy to memorize or easy to take a reminder from, and muddakir comes from the same root as dhikr, d-k-r.
